claim: Lesion studies have historically been instrumental for establishing causal connections between brain and behavior.
source: Lesion studies have historically been instrumental for establishing causal connections between brain and behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about the historical role of lesion studies in neuroscience, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Neuroelectrophysiology recording techniques with a large number of electrodes started developing in the 1970s.
source: The development of neuroelectrophysiology recording techniques with a large number of electrodes starting in the 1970s (Wise et al., 1970; Campbell et al., 1991; Campbell et al., 1990; Rios et al., 2016; Hong and Lieber, 2019) was a boon to systems neuroscience, enabling simultaneous recording from hundreds of neurons and revealing previously unseen aspects of population coding (Cunningham and Yu, 2014; Kalaska, 2019; Shenoy and Kao, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work documenting the development of these techniques.

claim: Prior to the last few decades, electrophysiology was limited to simultaneous recordings of at most five neurons with small numbers of electrodes.
source: Prior to the last few decades, electrophysiology was limited to simultaneous recordings of at most five neurons with small numbers of electrodes (typically one, two, or four) (McNaughton et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McNaughton et al., 1983.

claim: Over the last five years, electrode count has continued to increase, with new probes containing thousands of electrodes.
source: Over the last five years, electrode count has continued to increase, with new probes containing thousands of electrodes (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2021; Obaid et al., 2020; Sahasrabuddhe et al., 2021; Musk, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the development of high-density electrode probes.

claim: Novel tools that both record from and inactivate neurons are required to establish causal connections to behavior.
source: While experiments and analysis have revealed population activity that correlates strongly with behavioral output (Yu et al., 2009; Churchland et al., 2012; Sadtler et al., 2014; Golub et al., 2018; Elsayed et al., 2016; Goldman et al., 2019; Gallego et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Rasmussen et al., 2017), novel tools that both record from and inactivate neurons are required to establish causal connections to behavior (Vaidya et al., 2019; Shenoy and Kao, 2021; Slonina et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work discussing the need for combined recording and inactivation tools.

claim: A custom-built current source provides stable current and allows for controlled, repeatable lesions in awake-behaving animals.
source: A custom-built current source provides stable current and allows for controlled, repeatable lesions in awake-behaving animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including current traces and lesion outcomes.

claim: The circuit design is based on simple feedback control circuits using an operational amplifier to maintain a constant current.
source: The circuit design is based on simple feedback control circuits Texas Instruments Incorporated, 2019; Carter and Brown, 2016; Texas Instruments Incorporated, 2020 using an operational amplifier to maintain a constant current (Carter and Mancini, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to technical references on feedback control circuits and operational amplifiers.

claim: The circuit supplies the voltage needed to damage cortex while maintaining high precision in the delivered current with precision error not exceeding 10 μA.
source: Our circuit supplies the voltage needed to damage cortex while maintaining high precision in the delivered current (precision error not exceeding 10 μA).
evidence: This claim is supported by the design specifications and experimental measurements of the device.

claim: Sustained delivery of 250 μA of direct current for 10 min between adjacent electrodes resulted in a clean spheroidal cavitation in cortex approximately 1.5 mm in diameter in ex vivo sheep cortex.
source: Sustained delivery of 250 μA of direct current for 10 min between adjacent electrodes (400 μm spacing) resulted in a clean spheroidal cavitation in cortex approximately 1.5 mm in diameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by both the text description and Figure 2A and B showing the lesion.

claim: One minute of 180 μA direct current passed through two adjacent electrodes in ex vivo pig cortex created a smaller spheroidal cavitation of approximately 0.5 mm in diameter.
source: Reducing the duration and intensity of the current used to lesion created smaller cavitations in cortex: 1 min of 180 μA direct current, passed through two adjacent electrodes in ex vivo pig cortex, created a smaller spheroidal cavitation of approximately 0.5 mm in diameter (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the text description and Figure 2C showing the lesion.

claim: One minute of 150 μA direct current passed through two adjacent electrodes in pig cortex resulted in a well-demarcated region of parenchymal damage.
source: One minute of 150 μA direct current, passed through two adjacent electrodes in pig cortex resulted in a well-demarcated region of parenchymal damage (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the text description and Figure 3A showing the histology.

claim: The region of parenchymal damage was confined to an upside-down conical region, which was 3.5 mm wide at the cortical surface and extended approximately 2 mm deep.
source: The region of parenchymal damage appears paler on H&E staining than the adjacent, unaffected parenchyma and was confined to an upside-down conical region, which was 3.5 mm wide at the cortical surface and extended approximately 2 mm deep.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological measurements from Figure 3A.

claim: Within the damaged region, there was widespread coagulative necrosis, parenchymal rarefaction, and perivascular microhemorrhage.
source: Within this region (seen magnified in Figure 3B), there was widespread coagulative necrosis, parenchymal rarefaction, and perivascular microhemorrhage.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Acidophilic neuronal necrosis was identified along the marginal boundaries of the region of coagulative necrosis.
source: Acidophilic neuronal necrosis was identified along the marginal boundaries of the region of coagulative necrosis.
evidence: This claim is based on histological observations from the in vivo porcine testing.

claim: Adjacent neural parenchyma was unaffected, demonstrating the relatively precise boundary of damage caused by the electrolytic lesion.
source: Adjacent neural parenchyma was unaffected (representative selection shown in Figure 3C), demonstrating the relatively precise boundary of damage caused by the electrolytic lesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In control tests where a microelectrode array was inserted and removed but no current was used to create a lesion, regional coagulative necrosis was not present.
source: In control tests where a microelectrode array was inserted and removed but no current was used to create a lesion (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2), regional coagulative necrosis was not present, and cortical damage was conﬁned to mild subcortical and/or perivascular microhemmorhage and scattered individual neuronal necrosis, typically in regions adjacent to microvascular hemorrhage.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data documented in supplementary files.

claim: Electrolytic lesioning, not array insertion alone, leads to coagulative necrosis.
source: This emphasizes that electrolytic lesioning, not array insertion alone, leads to coagulative necrosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between lesion and control experiments.

claim: The electrolytic lesioning technique functions in any area of cortex in which a multielectrode probe can be implanted.
source: This testing was performed across many regions of porcine cortex, demonstrating that the electrolytic lesioning technique functions in any area of cortex in which a multielectrode probe can be implanted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental testing across multiple cortical regions in pigs.

claim: Fourteen lesions were performed across two awake-behaving rhesus macaques using thirteen unique electrode pairs.
source: This technique has since been used successfully in experimental settings with two other awake-behaving rhesus macaques (Monkeys H & U), for a total of fourteen lesions using thirteen unique electrode pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the in vivo rhesus macaque studies.

claim: As both the amplitude and duration of direct current increase, the volume of the lesion also increases.
source: We found that as both the amplitude and duration of direct current increase, the volume of the lesion also increases (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by lesion volume measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: As amplitude and duration of direct current decrease, the type of damage changes from cavitation to rarefied tissue damage.
source: We also found that as amplitude and duration of direct current decrease, the type of damage changes (Figure 5). While lesions with larger current amplitudes and durations create cavitations in cortex (as in all of the ex vivo and the longest in vivo lesion), lesions where the current had a lower amplitude and/or was applied for a shorter duration resulted in rarefied tissue damage (as seen in Figure 3), containing parenchymal rarefaction, coagulative necrosis, and perivascular microhemorrhage.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations across different lesion parameters shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The current source worked as expected, providing a constant current throughout the duration of the procedure in all fourteen lesions across two awake-behaving rhesus macaques.
source: In all of the fourteen lesions across two awake-behaving rhesus macaques (150 μA direct current passed through adjacent electrodes for 30 or 45 s [30 s for Monkey U and 45 s for Monkey H, except lesion H200120 which was for 50 s]), the current source worked as expected, providing a constant current throughout the duration of the procedure.
evidence: This claim is supported by current measurements from the device during lesioning procedures.

claim: Fluctuations in current amplitude were likely due to the 10 μA precision of the multimeter used to read out the current.
source: Fluctuations in current amplitude were likely due to the 10 μA precision of the multimeter used to read out the current (e.g. the readout would sometimes switch between 150 μA and 160 μA).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known precision limitations of the measurement device.

claim: The voltage across the microelectrode array fluctuated much more than the current did.
source: The voltage across the microelectrode array ﬂuctuated much more than the current did, emphasizing that we made the correct choice in using a current source to ensure delivery of consistent amounts of current into the brain (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage and current traces shown in Figure 6.

claim: Upon turning on the lesioning device, the voltage initially increased sharply, sometimes exceeding the slew rate of the voltmeter.
source: Upon turning on the lesioning device, the voltage initially increased sharply, sometimes exceeding the slew rate of the voltmeter (seen as a discontinuity in the traces in Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage traces shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After the initial voltage peak, the voltage predominantly levels off.
source: After this peak, the voltage predominantly levels off.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage traces shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After the power to the boost converter is removed, the current supplied by the circuit briefly persists, likely due to residual energy present in the capacitors of the boost converter downstream of the switch.
source: However, after the power to the boost converter is removed, the current supplied by the circuit brieﬂy persists — likely due to residual energy present in the capacitors of the boost converter downstream of the switch.
evidence: This is an inference based on circuit design principles and observed current persistence.

claim: In nine out of the fourteen lesions performed in two awake rhesus macaques, the current value was higher than what was calibrated.
source: In nine out of the fourteen lesions performed in two awake rhesus macaques (thirteen of which had this voltage data collected), the current value was higher than what was calibrated.
evidence: This claim is supported by current measurements during lesioning procedures.

claim: A parasitic parallel resistance to ground through the animal itself could explain the 10-20 μA increase in current above the set value.
source: We hypothesize that this is due to a parasitic parallel resistance to ground through the animal itself (see dashed box in Figure 1). To have created the 10–20 μA increase in current above the set value, this parasitic parallel resistance would have been between 1.2 MΩ and 0.6 MΩ, respectively, which is in the range of the expected resistance when the body is in dry contact with the environment (Fish and Geddes, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by circuit analysis and cited literature on body resistance.

claim: Microelectrode arrays were able to continue recording stable neuronal activity in awake-behaving rhesus after multiple lesions.
source: Comparisons of the recorded action potential waveforms before and after multiple lesions revealed that microelectrode arrays were able to continue recording stable neuronal activity in awake-behaving rhesus (e.g. after one lesion performed in Monkey U and after six lesions performed in Monkey H; Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Even the lesion electrodes themselves continued to record reliably after lesioning.
source: Surprisingly, even the lesion electrodes themselves continued to record reliably, suggesting that the modest electrolytic lesion intensity used is not prohibitively destructive to an electrode's recording ability.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from lesion electrodes shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Rates of turnover in the recorded population had been accelerated by the lesion.
source: These values dropped below the expected percentage of matching neurons among pre- and post-lesion days (pre-pre, post-post) confirming that rates of turnover in the recorded population had been accelerated by the lesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neuron turnover shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: The electrolytic lesioning device can deliver steady current through a Plexon U-Probe linear electrode.
source: This testing demonstrates the ability to deliver steady current through a different multielectrode probe from the Utah microelectrode array, which was the primary probe used in most of these experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental testing with the U-Probe shown in Figure 8.

claim: Five distinct lesions were created through contiguous contacts of a U-Probe by applying differing current amplitudes (240 μA and 150 μA) for differing durations (30, 60, and 120 s) in ex vivo rabbit cortex.
source: Using our original electrolytic lesioning device and the U-Probe, we created five distinct lesions through contiguous contacts (100 μm apart) by applying differing current amplitudes (240 μA and 150 μA) for differing durations (30, 60, and 120 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo rabbit cortex testing shown in Figure 8.

claim: Electrolytic lesioning leads to cell death through heat, electroporation, and local changes in pH.
source: Electrolytic lesioning leads to cell death through heat (Nikfarjam et al., 2005), electroporation Batista Napotnik et al., 2021), and local changes in pH (Nikfarjam et al., 2005.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on mechanisms of electrolytic lesioning.

claim: Temporary increases in the day-to-day turnover of recorded waveforms were observed after lesioning.
source: Temporary increases in the day-to-day turnover of recorded waveforms were observed after lesioning (i.e. decreases in the percent of matching neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Significant neuronal loss is likely occurring just outside of the array electrodes' recording volume and thus evading detection.
source: On one hand, this is likely an underestimate, as significant neuronal loss is likely occurring just outside of the array electrodes' recording volume and thus evading detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial limitations of electrode recording ranges.

claim: Many of the array's electrodes are recording smaller inseparable waveforms (hash) corresponding to many different neurons located between 50 μm and 140 μm from the electrode tip before the lesion.
source: It is evident in our recordings that many of the array's electrodes are recording smaller inseparable waveforms (hash) corresponding to many different neurons located between between 50 μm and 140 μm from the electrode tip before the lesion (Buzsáki, 2004; Gerstein and Clark, 1964).
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological recordings and cited literature on recording ranges.

claim: Larger ablations are theoretically possible by supplying larger currents or performing a lesion over non-adjacent electrodes, which can span as much as 5.6 mm for electrodes on the opposite corners of the 4 mm x 4 mm Utah array.
source: In theory, larger ablations are possible by supplying larger currents or performing a lesion over non-adjacent electrodes, which can span as much as 5.6 mm for electrodes on the opposite corners of the 4 mm x 4 mm Utah array.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the geometry of the Utah array and circuit capabilities.

claim: The main requirements for use of the electrolytic lesioning device are that the probe has two electrodes that can directly connect to the lesioning device, such that arbitrary current can be passed into them as the anode and cathode.
source: The main requirements for use are that the probe has two electrodes that can directly (via whatever necessary adapters) connect to the lesioning device, such that arbitrary current can be passed into them as the anode and cathode.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical requirements for using the device.

claim: The specific op amp used has a voltage range of ±450 V, which assuming a desired output of 150 μA of current would limit electrode impedance to 6 MΩ.
source: The specific op amp used here has a voltage range of ±450 V, which assuming a desired output of 150 μA of current would limit electrode impedance to 6 MΩ.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the op amp specifications and Ohm's law.

claim: Most electrodes have impedances between 100 kΩ to 1 MΩ.
source: Although a different op amp could easily be used to accommodate a higher electrode impedance, it is unlikely that this would be necessary, since most electrodes have impedances between 100 kΩ to 1 MΩ (Maynard et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on electrode impedances.

claim: The total cost of the parts needed for the lesioning device is approximately three hundred US dollars.
source: The total cost of the parts needed is approximately three hundred US dollars, making it an affordable addition to a neuroelectrophysiology recording setup.
evidence: This is a statement about the cost of building the device.

claim: All lesioning was performed using Utah electrode arrays with the same specifications: 4 mm x 4 mm, with 96 channels, electrode shafts made of silicon with a metallic outer layer (platinum or platinum-iridium), coated with parylene-C, 1 mm in length with 400 μm inter-electrode spacing.
source: All lesioning was performed using Utah electrode arrays with the same specifications (Blackrock Neurotech, Salt Lake City, UT). The arrays are 4 mmx4 mm, with 96 channels. Electrode shafts are made of silicon (Si) with a metallic outer layer (platinum or platinum-iridium), and coated with parylene-C. Electrodes are 1 mm in length and have a 400 μm inter-electrode spacing.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials used.

claim: Across eleven ex vivo and five in vivo animals, 61 lesions were performed, including some repeated parameter combinations as biological replicates.
source: Across eleven ex vivo and five in vivo animals, 61 lesions were performed, including some repeated parameter combinations as biological replicates.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental sample size.

claim: Pilot studies were performed in sheep and pigs in accordance with the guidelines of the National Research Council, 2003; National Research Council, 2011 of replacement, refinement, and reduction (3 R's).
source: Although scientific use of this lesioning device is ultimately intended in rhesus, pilot studies were performed in sheep and pigs in accordance with the guidelines of the National Research Council, 2003; National Research Council, 2011 of replacement, refinement, and reduction (3 R's).
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical considerations in experimental design.

claim: Prior studies demonstrated that 20 min of 400 μA direct current resulted in a spherical cavitation in cortex of approximately 2 mm in diameter.
source: Prior studies demonstrated that 20 min of 400 μA direct current resulted in a spherical cavitation in cortex of approximately 2 mm in diameter (Wurtz and Goldberg, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Lesions of approximately 1.5 mm in diameter are known to cause significant behavioral deficits.
source: This created a clean spheroidal cavitation in cortex approximately 1.5 mm in diameter (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B), which is consistent with lesion sizes that cause measurable behavioral deficits in the motor system (Nudo et al., 2003; Wurtz and Goldberg, 1972; Glees and Cole, 1950).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on lesion-behavior relationships.

claim: Electrolytic lesioning is not painful as there are no direct pain receptors in the central nervous system.
source: Electrolytic lesioning is not painful as there are no direct pain receptors in the central nervous system (Hall and Hall, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on pain physiology.

claim: All animal procedures and protocols were approved by the Stanford University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (#D16-00134).
source: All animal procedures and protocols were approved by the Stanford University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (#D16-00134).
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory approval for the research.

claim: Action potentials were identified by thresholding the filtered membrane potential at −4× the root mean square voltage measured over the first minute of the recording session.
source: Action potentials were identified by thresholding the ﬁltered membrane potential at −4× the root mean square voltage measured over the first minute of the recording session.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods used.

claim: Waveforms whose peak-to-trough amplitude exceeded 300 μV are atypical of extracellular recordings from cortical neurons using Utah arrays and were excluded.
source: Waveforms whose peak-to-trough amplitude exceeded 300 μV are atypical of extracellular recordings from cortical neurons using Utah arrays and were excluded (Chestek et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on typical waveform characteristics.

claim: Unphysiological waveforms whose widths were longer than 1ms were excluded.
source: Unphysiological waveforms whose widths were longer than 1ms were also excluded (Bean, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on physiological waveform characteristics.
